WorkedExamples.Title: Source-student probability and sampling task — Chance Experiments
WorkedExamples.Question: A fair bag has 3 blue balls, 2 red balls, and no green balls; a ball is drawn without looking. Classify drawing green, blue, or red and explain all categories.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify sample space, actual versus illustrative data and study design; create a student-sourced table, tree or graph, then justify the probability or estimate.
Steps: Five equally likely balls are in the bag.
P(blue)=3/5=0.6, so more likely than not; P(red)=2/5=0.4, so less likely than not.

WorkedExamples.Answer: Green impossible; blue likely; red unlikely; blue-or-red certain.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks probability number line and language nuance.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-student probability and sampling task — Memory Test
WorkedExamples.Question: A 10-by-10 anonymous score grid has 100 values. Compare selecting 20 uniformly random distinct cells versus selecting the first 20 values or a contiguous path of 20.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify sample space, actual versus illustrative data and study design; create a student-sourced table, tree or graph, then justify the probability or estimate.
Steps: Uniform sampling without replacement can give every cell equal inclusion probability 20/100.
The first 20 values may systematically reflect ordering, and a contiguous path can preserve local clustering.
Choose 20 distinct cell indices by a uniform random method, record their actual values and calculate the sample summary.
Compare a new independent random draw; avoid asserting causal effects from scores without an experimental design.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A genuinely uniform 20-cell sample is defensible; first-20 or linked paths are not automatically representative.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks a real reproducible selection protocol and the sampled-value calculations.
